question: How does my heart beat?
teaser: Open the heart, find its pacemaker, and follow the signal down to the muscle cells and the molecule that powers them.

stops.title: Your body
text: In the middle of your chest, slightly to the left, is a fist-sized muscle. It squeezes about 100,000 times a day to push blood around your body.
Over a lifetime that adds up to roughly 2.5 to 3 billion beats.
stops.model: An anatomical model of an average adult. The positions of organs are typical, not those of any one person.
stops.notice: Choose "Organs" at the top to see what lies behind the ribs.

stops.title: Inside the heart
text: The heart is a pump with four chambers. It weighs about 250 to 350 grams, and it moves roughly 5 litres of blood a minute.
Valves between the chambers are one-way doors, so the blood always moves in the same direction.
stops.model: The heart is cut open for a view of the inside. Structures are typical, not copied from one person.
stops.notice: Click the chambers and valves to read what each one does.

stops.title: The pacemaker
text: The beat does not wait for a signal from the brain. A small cluster of special cells in the right atrium, the sinoatrial node, sets the rhythm.
Each time it fires, an electrical signal spreads through the muscle and makes it squeeze.
stops.notice: Find the marked point in the right atrium, the pacemaker.

stops.title: One heartbeat
text: A beat has two phases: the heart relaxes and fills with blood, and then it squeezes to push blood out. At 75 beats a minute the whole cycle takes about 0.8 seconds.
The left chamber holds about 120 millilitres when full, and squeezes out roughly 55 to 70 percent of that each beat.
stops.notice: Read the numbers on the card, then count your own pulse for fifteen seconds and multiply by four.

stops.title: Heart muscle
text: Heart muscle is made of cells that are striped, branched and joined end to end, so a signal can pass from one to the next. Each cell is about 100 micrometres long.
About 30 percent of the volume of a heart muscle cell is mitochondria, which release energy from food. The heart never rests, so it needs a constant supply.
stops.model: A generic illustration of muscle tissue, not a micrograph. The cells are drawn as plain rods: real heart cells are striped and branched.
stops.notice: Each rod stands for one muscle cell, about 100 micrometres long. Notice how they lie side by side in bundles, so that they can pull together.

stops.title: The contracting machine
text: Inside each cell are stacks of tiny protein motors called sarcomeres, each about 2.2 to 2.5 micrometres long. A signal makes calcium flood the cell, and the motors pull thin filaments past thick ones.
Each pull moves the filament about 5 to 10 nanometres. Millions of them at once shorten the cell, and so squeeze the heart.
stops.notice: Read the card: each little motor needs ATP to pull.

stops.title: The fuel
text: The motors run on a molecule called ATP, the cell's energy currency. A cell splits a phosphate off ATP to power work, and rebuilds the ATP from food.
The body holds only about 50 grams of ATP at a time, but it turns over about 50 to 70 kilograms of it a day.
stops.model: A ball-and-stick picture of one molecule. Bond lengths are true, but the atoms are drawn smaller than their real size so that the bonds show, and the colours are a convention, not real colours.
stops.notice: Find the chain of three phosphate groups at one end. Breaking off the last one is what releases the energy.

answer: Your heart beats because a pacemaker in it fires regular electrical signals that make its muscle cells contract together, powered by ATP made in their mitochondria.
unknown: The beat is well understood. What is still studied is why the rhythm sometimes fails, and how to repair damaged heart muscle, which does not regrow much.
